title: The plowed field
hookLine: he sees worms turned up by the plow and feels grief for them; then meets a wanderer (Buddhacarita 5)

lines: SMALL LIVES IN THE OPEN AIR.
cards: Fresh soil, turned over in long rows. If you've ever dug a garden bed, you've seen what comes up with it: worms, grubs, beetles, small things suddenly in the open air, some of them cut in half by the blade.
The prince, riding out toward the forest, stops his horse at the edge of a plowed field and looks. And the poem says what he feels. Not disgust.
Not curiosity. Grief, the kind a person feels for family.

teach.b: First, the field. The ground has been torn by the plow, the young grass ripped up, and the earth is strewn with tiny creatures, insects and worms, killed or dying.
The prince grieves, the poem says, as if his own kin had been slain. Second, the people.
He sees the plowmen too, their bodies darkened by wind and sun and dust, and the oxen worn out from dragging the plow. The same mercy falls on all of them. Nobody in the field is the villain.
Everyone in it is suffering something. Third, the stillness.
He gets down from his horse, walks, sorrowful, and sits beneath a rose-apple tree. There he thinks about birth and death in the world, and his mind grows quiet and clear.
The poem describes him settling into the first stage of deep meditation, right at the edge of a working field. And fourth, the visitor.
A figure in a wanderer's robe comes toward him, someone the poem says no one else can see. He has left home, he says, afraid of birth and death, to seek freedom.
Then, the poem says, he rises into the sky and is gone: a god in disguise, come to show the prince the road. So the poem joins the field and the fourth sight into one scene.
First the grief, then the calm under the tree, and only then the wanderer, as if the prince had to feel for the smallest lives before he could see the way out for all of them.

how: Care for small creatures runs through Buddhist practice: the first precept is to refrain from taking life, and in some monastic traditions monks strain their drinking water or take care where they walk to avoid harming insects.

o: a numb calm that stops you caring for others
a quiet, clear mind settling into meditation
keeping the body motionless for hours

games.q: the field in the poem: tap the pairs.
p: worn by sun, dust and work

s: in the poem, the prince grieves only for the worms
he also sees the tired plowmen and worn-out oxen.
the wanderer is seen by everyone in the field
the poem says no one else can see him.
the prince grows calm under a rose-apple tree
he settles into deep meditation at the edge of the field.

games.q: you're riding past a freshly plowed field. the soil is full of torn worms and insects. what do you do?
o: ride on; it's just a field.
stop, get down, and let the grief in.
games.why: he grieves as if for his own kin, then walks, and sits beneath a rose-apple tree until his mind is calm.

practice: Look at the ground near you, a floor, a lawn, a windowsill, or close your eyes and bring one to mind, and find something tiny that's alive: an ant, a spider, a moss, a weed pushing up.
Watch it for a while, and let it be as real to you as a person would be. No need to rescue it or name it; just give it your full attention, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: stillness. What comes to the prince beneath a rose-apple tree after grieving for the worms turned up by the plow: a quiet, clear mind, and the first stage of deep meditation. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: grief for the small. The calm came after the caring. Day seven hundred five, done.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 5 (the plowed field, the rose-apple tree, the wanderer)
